articles.title: Contract Review Workspaces in 2026: 3-Layer Retrieval Recovery Ledger
articles.excerpt: Short answer: build legal contract review retrieval around a replayable evidence ledger, then retain three different layers for three different periods: source revisions for authority, retrieval recei…
articles.body: Short answer: build legal contract review retrieval around a replayable evidence ledger, then retain three different layers for three different periods: source revisions for authority, retrieval receipts for audit and replay, and replaceable index artifacts only for fast service restoration. That choice puts the expensive question in the right place. The bill is not merely the vector index. It is the sum of source retention, parsed text, embeddings, lexical and vector replicas, reranking work, query receipts, and the engineering time required to prove why a clause appeared in a review. In a contract workspace, I would first measure stored bytes by artifact class and retrieval compute by stage. Don't optimize a per-query detail while duplicate index generations dominate storage.

articles.title: Alpha vs Solid Fill: Choosing a Background Removal Output
articles.excerpt: A cutout can look perfect against a checkerboard background and still look wrong when placed on an actual page. In many cases, the problem comes down to the output format. Choose the format based on w…
articles.body: A cutout can look perfect against a checkerboard background and still look wrong when placed on an actual page. In many cases, the problem comes down to the output format. Choose the format based on where the image will be used: Use a transparent PNG (with an alpha channel) when the subject needs to work on different backgrounds. Preserve the soft pixels around the edges. Cutting them off too aggressively can create a visible halo. Use WebP or JPEG with a solid background when the destination is fixed, such as a product grid. You can merge the background into the image once instead of carrying around a large alpha channel. Check the result at its actual display size. Edge artifacts that are hard to notice at full resolution can become obvious fringes in a thumbnail.

articles.title: United vs Southwest: Two Very Different Bets on AI Flight Booking

articles.body: A traveler asks an AI assistant to find a flight, compare the options, and buy the best ticket. One airline says third-party agents should stay out of its booking system. Another has put flight shopping inside ChatGPT, while still sending customers to its own website to pay. Those choices look like opposite reactions to AI. The real difference is how much of the journey each airline lets an assistant handle and who gets to approve the final step. That distinction matters more than the headline word "ban." It points to a design question every company with customer accounts will face: should an AI act through a customer's existing login, or should it use a limited, approved connection built for the task?

articles.title: Polling vs Webhooks for a Personal Stripe Revenue Widget: Why I Chose Polling
articles.excerpt: When you build a small tool that shows your own Stripe revenue, the first design question is how it learns about new payments. Webhooks feel like the "proper" answer. For a personal desktop widget, I…
articles.body: When you build a small tool that shows your own Stripe revenue, the first design question is how it learns about new payments. Webhooks feel like the "proper" answer. For a personal desktop widget, I think polling is usually the better fit. What webhooks need Stripe webhooks call a public HTTPS endpoint. A desktop app on a laptop has no stable public address, so you need a server or relay in the middle. That server now receives your payment events, needs its own secrets, uptime and logging, and becomes one more place your revenue data passes through. What polling needs Polling only needs the app to call the Stripe API on a schedule with a key it already has.

articles.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
articles.excerpt: A hidden black hole or neutron star companion to an unstable massive star is causing the system to erupt in light that mimics a supernova explosion.
articles.body: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 12, 2014: European Philae probe lands on Comet 67P, bounced twice and then got lost for nearly 2 years
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P, then bounced twice and got lost. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement. The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired. When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down. Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

articles.body: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China.

articles.body: 4 Min Read I Am Artemis Katie Spicer For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history. NASA’s Katie Spicer stands in front of the crew cabin prototype for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lunar lander. The lander is one of two commercial human landing systems that will help safely ferry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for the agency’s crewed Artemis missions in 2028.
